US science academy urges journals to fix errors more rapidly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J.
  • Science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds.
  • Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J. Richards/AFP via Getty.

Science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds. Standards for fixing errors are also inconsistently applied across research journals, it says.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science.

Industry observers note that there are no data on how long retraction or correction presently takes, as journals do not generally disclose when they were alerted to a problem in a paper; the NASEM report claims they should. On average, according to the Retraction Watch database, retractions occur around 2.4 years after a paper is published. The report recommends that editorial review processes be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months — at least when editors are looking at concerns over a single paper.

“The major picture is, the process is too slow,” says Randy Schekman, a cell biologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who chaired the 14-person committee that produced the NASEM report. A prompter and more transparent process would strengthen the reliability of the scientific record, he says.

The report was due to be published online on 19 November, but publication was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained some references with fabricated first names for authors, a possible sign that large language models had been used to write or edit the material and had been insufficiently checked.

“It's unfortunate that there were these flawed references in a report about fixing the literature,” states Jennifer Byrne, a cancer researcher and research integrity sleuth at the University of Sydney who first flagged the concern to Science when reviewing the report, which was shared ahead of publication with media outlets.

The report had two main aims: to speed up the process of retraction or correction and to lower the “tremendous emotional barriers” for authors to correct honest mistakes in the record, Schekman indicates. “Part of the problem is that it’s too rare for a paper to be retracted,” he adds.

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Sources indicate that the report also suggests that journals shouldn’t just wait for complaints to reach them, but instead “take proactive steps” to identify errors and integrity challenges. That might include journal-wide audits, or regularly monitoring social media and online platforms where post-publication issues are raised, it says.

Existing guidelines for publishers, such as those from the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in London, only urge a “timely” response to concerns without setting out expected schedules, and don’t suggest journals scan online platforms for complaints.

Recent findings suggest that “A major theme running through the report is that we have to distinguish between retraction or correction, and research misconduct,” notes Dorothy Bishop, a research-integrity sleuth in Oxford, UK, who was on the NASEM committee. Authors shouldn’t associate retracting a paper with the stigma of misconduct, she states. And although journal editors sometimes wait for a university to investigate whether there is research misconduct before correcting a paper, they shouldn’t, she adds.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a newly introduced record.

Calls for changing these attitudes aren’t new: journals have long emphasized that retractions can cover honest mistakes. When it comes to journal processes, Holden Thorpe, the editor in chief of Science, urged that issuing corrections or retractions and making a determination of misconduct be separated in an editorial in 2022, and COPE guidelines already emphasize the point. But “there are still plenty of people who see a correction or retraction as an allegation of fraud,” claims Thorpe, who was also on the NASEM committee. “Hopefully, this report will accelerate the recognition of the distinction,” he says.

Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.
  • In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.
  • Recent findings suggest that still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," stated Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Recent findings suggest that still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," stated Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate prepares, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy.".

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

Industry observers note that "We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum.".

According to recent reports, that momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," mentioned CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey remarked Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

Industry observers note that the only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

Recent findings suggest that the G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low.".

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

In a recent development, however, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, stated the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action.".

This article was originally published in German.

According to Sky, Calhanoglu is already certain to miss Inter’s next two games: against Stuttgart in the Champions League and Genoa in Serie A.

Calhanoglu was subbed off during the first half of Inter’s 4-4 draw against Atalanta on Sunday.

Piotr Zielinski was also injured, so Calhanoglu was replaced by Petar Sucic, and the Croatian scored a penalty in the second half to restore Inter’s two-goal lead, which didn’t last until the end of the game.

Calhanoglu, 32, already missed five games for club and country from mid-September to early October due to an adductor injury.

The Turkey international has scored three goals in ten appearances across all competitions this season, and his contract expires this coming June.

#94901. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's vital.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (958 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's vital.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black?
  • Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?
  • Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Your brain has its own version of that.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

It has been revealed that but to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

It has been revealed that they noticed that when participants started to focus on a upcoming task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

In a recent development, it turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's crucial to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

Industry observers note that there's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?".

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice vital signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

Sources indicate that and the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

The DMN is not always necessarily good.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great newly introduced idea.

In a recent development, but it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

According to recent reports, scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

It has been revealed that protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

In a recent development, take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Embrace boredom and enjoy doing nothing.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

In a recent development, try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

Everton’s return to Premier League action proved a forgettable one as a 17-minute first-half spell ultimately condemned them to a 4-0 defeat at Brentford.

Looking to extend their three-match unbeaten run built before the recent international break, the Blues struggled to get going at the Gtech Stadium – before rotten luck left them with a mountain to climb.

On 23 minutes, Keane Lewis-Potter’s run into the area was picked out by Jaidon Anthony as his finish took a horrible deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite to beat Jordan Pickford.

Worse misfortune struck Everton two minutes later as Lewis-Potter’s shot was blocked by James Tarkowski, fell straight back into the path of the same Brentford player whose rebound was destined to be kept out again, only to hit Thierno Barry and wrong-foot Pickford.

The Toffees’ hopes of mounting a comeback were then all but ended five minutes before the interval when Tarkowski was penalised for a sliding tackle on Yehor Yarmoliuk.

Initially slow to award the free-kick, referee Craig Pawson eventually showed the Blues captain a yellow card – only to be called over by VAR and soon change his decision to red for violent conduct.

Left to battle on with 10 men, Everton had a sniff of a comeback with seconds left of the first half when fine work from Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall ended with the No.8 chipping in a cross that Barry did well to nod into the bottom right-hand corner, only for keeper Caoimhin Kelleher to somehow claw the ball away.

Jack Grealish came on for the start of the second half and soon made an impact with a teasing centre across the six-yard box that just evaded Barry.

But any hopes of an unlikely fightback were ended on 67 minutes as Vitaly Janelt fired a 25-yard strike into the top right-hand corner.

And a miserable night was summed up in the dying moments when Damsgaard's corner found its way to substitute Fabio Carvalho to tap over the line from a yard out.

  • The World Cup is set to return to America after FIFA awarded the 2031 women's tournament to a historic four-nation bid.
  • Following the success of the men's tournament this summer, the United States was announced as one of the hosts of the women's edition in five years' time during a virtual meeting of FIFA's national associations on Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By ISABEL BALDWIN, US ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 10:23 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 13:19 EST, 23 November 2026.

The World Cup is set to return to America after FIFA awarded the 2031 women's tournament to a historic four-nation bid.

Following the success of the men's tournament this summer, the United States was announced as one of the hosts of the women's edition in five years' time during a virtual meeting of FIFA's national associations on Monday.

The US will co-host the global soccer extravaganza alongside Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica after the four countries' joint bid was awarded uncontested the 2031 tournament.

The selection marks a milestone for the Women's World Cup with the tournament being hosted across four nations for the first time in its history.

The last World Cup was co-hosted by multiple countries for the first time with the 2023 edition taking place across Australia and Newly introduced Zealand.

This summer's men's World Cup was also co-hosted by the US with games taking place across the States, Canada and Mexico.

The World Cup is set to return to the United States for the 2031 women's edition of the event.

Spain are reigning champions after winning the Women's World Cup in 2023.

The United States Women's National Team are four-time winners in 1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019.

The 2031 tournament will also be the largest in the competition's history, featuring an expanded 48-team field and 104 matches for the first time.

'We are incredibly honored and excited to welcome the world to the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica for the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup,' stated US Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone.

According to recent reports, 'This is a historic moment for our four countries, but the opportunity is much bigger than any one of us. Together with FIFA, we want to deliver the biggest and most impactful Women's World Cup in history and use its success to accelerate the growth of women's soccer around the world. Our ambition is to create a tournament that not only inspires millions of players, but helps give them the opportunities to play, grow and pursue their dreams.'.

The selection marks the third time that the Women's World Cup has been awarded to the US with the country previously hosting the landmark 1999 and 2003 editions alone. The national team's tournament win in 1999 was the second of its four titles.

Meanwhile, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will become first-time hosts at the historic tournament.

'This milestone furthers the continued belief that the best days of soccer in America are still ahead,' mentioned U.S. Soccer CEO and General Secretary JT Batson.

Sources indicate that 'We have an opportunity to use the momentum from the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup to accelerate our ambitions for the future of soccer, from expanding access and participation to strengthening the pathways that develop the next generation of players. We are excited to work alongside our partners across the region to make this tournament a defining moment for women's soccer.'.

The U.S.-led 2031 project across the CONCACAF regional soccer body bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

US Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone said the federation was honored to be selected.

The host selection of the 2035 Women's World Cup was awarded to a joint bid between England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

The host selection of the 2035 Women's World Cup was also unveiled on Monday with the tournament being awarded to another joint bid between England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

It marks the first time that a World Cup has been hosted on the British Isles since the men's tournament in 1966 in England.

The United Kingdom bid joins England with Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales that offers a choice from 19 venues, including Wembley Stadium in London.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments - the first editions with 48 teams and 104 games - and to reinvest all that money in women's soccer.

In a recent development, FIFA wanted these heavyweights of women's soccer to face no opposition without rival bids and so lead hosting the first expanded tournaments. That will bring parity with the men's World Cup which expanded to 48 teams this year in the US, Canada and Mexico.

The 2027 Women's World Cup will have 32 teams in Brazil.

Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.
  • "The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he noted, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he noted, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

According to recent reports, A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres remarked the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach.".

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he stated, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including major polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest.".

Sources indicate that "Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she noted, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

According to recent reports, most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, remarked the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and swiftly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over.".

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," mentioned Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

Recent findings suggest that "We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most.".

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she stated, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Recent findings suggest that iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian noted his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the matter to climate finance and stated his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms.".

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, remarked the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

In a recent development, he also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he mentioned.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

According to recent reports, eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”.

According to recent reports, this was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and mentioned “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM.

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

Sources indicate that the anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Sources indicate that arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”.

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

Industry observers note that it was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Industry observers note that salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

Could the miracle happen? When half-time arrived with Fleetwood still in the lead, you began to wonder. But then you saw Ben White and Martin Odegaard go through intense warm-ups so they could be introduced at the start of the second half and you knew the mountain had become taller.

So it proved. #94889. Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.
  • For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.
  • In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.

In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.

The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.

Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.

However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.

The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism.

The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank noted in response to a query from DW.

Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said.

According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts.".

But critics see this as a major weakness.

"The mechanism must be easily accessible," noted Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

Recent findings suggest that she argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

Industry observers note that the AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it stated, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.

Sources indicate that urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

Industry observers note that for 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

In a recent development, "The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly crucial documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," stated Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, noted the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough.".

Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he stated, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.

Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not upcoming. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.

The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.

For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that as of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

But Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles.".

The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive.".

The newly introduced rules have been in effect for only 10 months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank stated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Steinert remarked fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.

Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.

Recent findings suggest that such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert said. However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.

The bank remarked that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns.".

"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.

Sausmikat said Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

According to recent reports, hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards.".

This article was originally written in German.

Sleuth finds ‘impossible proteins’ in hundreds of research papers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, some studies show the expression of proteins such as caspase-3 (pictured), in cell lines that should not be able to produce them.
  • Recent findings suggest that A scientific sleuth has identified more than 220 research papers that describe impossible patterns of protein expression in genetically altered cell lines.
  • Journals are now taking action to clean up the literature by retracting or correcting the work, and researchers warn that there are probably many more affected studies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, some studies show the expression of proteins such as caspase-3 (pictured), in cell lines that should not be able to produce them. Credit: Dr Mark J. Winter/Science Photo Library.

Recent findings suggest that A scientific sleuth has identified more than 220 research papers that describe impossible patterns of protein expression in genetically altered cell lines. In these studies, particular proteins show up in imaging experiments, even though the cells do not have the gene necessary to make them.

Journals are now taking action to clean up the literature by retracting or correcting the work, and researchers warn that there are probably many more affected studies.

According to recent reports, “This problem will not go away,” indicates Thierry Soussi, a cancer geneticist at Uppsala University in Sweden, who notes that there are several other examples of the issue in now-retracted papers that were not included in the sleuth’s analysis. “This is only the tip of a gigantic iceberg.”.

Cell lines are groups of cells derived from a single origin cell and cultured for use in experiments. Some cancer cell lines have been genetically modified with mutations and deletions — often to remove genes that usually control cell division. This means that the cultures continually divide and grow, giving researchers the chance to study tumour progression and test potential treatments.

In a recent development, the MCF-7 cell line is one of these. It lacks the gene for caspase-3 protein, which is involved in cell death. In 2009, researchers warned1 that some studies that report working with MCF-7 have mysteriously observed caspase-3 expression in western blots, an imaging technique that identifies proteins based on their molecular weight.

Sleuth identifies dozens of studies that used the wrong antibody.

Sleuth identifies dozens of studies that used the wrong antibody.

In the most recent analysis, published as a preprint on 21 October to the data repository Zenodo2, Sholto David, a sleuth based in Arbroath, UK, finds that this problem persists and extends to other cell lines.

David compiled a list of 20 commonly used cell lines with genetic mutations or deletions that leave cells unable to express specific proteins. He then scoured the literature using Google text and image searches to identify examples of western-blot images that unexpectedly identify these proteins. He also searched a collection of 140,000 articles that he had previously downloaded and screened for image-integrity issues and other problems, most of which were biomedicine papers.

Sources indicate that he found 230 reports of phantom proteins across 221 papers published since 2004. The most common errors were observations of caspase-3 expression in the MCF-7 cell line, affecting 49 papers; expression of the cell-death protein BAX in the Jurkat cell line in 47 papers; and expression of the signalling protein STAT3 in the PC-3 cell line in 35 papers.

It has been revealed that david suggests several explanations for these impossible protein-expression patterns. They might be the result of honest errors: researchers could have misidentified the cell lines or contaminated them with others. Or the antibodies used to identify proteins in the western-blot experiments could have been non-specific and bound to another protein with the same molecular weight. In fact, David says that he stumbled across the anomalous proteins while working on a project that flagged hundreds of studies that used the wrong antibodies in experiments.

According to recent reports, another possibility is that some of the papers are the product of papermills, companies that fabricate and sell scientific manuscripts. David indicates that some papers in the cache contain the hallmarks of being produced by such outfits, including duplicated images or text templates that are similar to other papers. The proportion of the papers that fall into this category is not clear, he says.

Nature has contacted several authors of papers containing anomalies to ask for comment, but none responded.

Science sleuths raise concerns about scores of bioengineering papers.

#94881. Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds

Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work.
  • According to recent reports, across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often.
  • The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a upcoming study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

According to recent reports, across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

In a recent development, since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, claims women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

According to recent reports, the researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial firm in China.

In a recent development, intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

In a recent development, the effects were small, and the study highlights a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

Recent findings suggest that in both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

It has been revealed that no, Chawla states. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw.".

In a recent development, small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she stated.

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she states, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she claims: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

Three Italian players are set for lengthy spells on the sidelines after the latest round of Serie A fixtures, including two members of Roberto Mancini’s most recent national team squad.

Napoli’s Antonio Vergara, Atalanta’s Marco Carnesecchi and Genoa’s Lorenzo Colombo are all expected to miss several months of action with serious injuries they suffered during the 12th round of 2026-27 Serie A fixtures.

Vergara was visibly distressed when he was forced out of Napoli’s 1-0 win over Torino, making way for Kevin De Bruyne after just 11 minutes.

Napoli confirmed in a statement on Monday that he has undergone medical tests that have revealed a high-grade tear to the biceps femoris muscle in his left thigh and according to reports from Sky Sport Italia, this will keep him out of action for a minimum of two months. Other outlets suggest that the timeline will be closer to three months.

Atalanta stopper Carnesecchi, meanwhile, is due to undergo surgery on his knee on Tuesday after suffering a tear of the medial meniscus in his left knee after pulling up injured in the warm-up of his side’s 4-4 draw against Inter on Sunday evening.

It remains unclear exactly how long the 26-year-old will miss, but initial reports suggest that he will be ruled out until January at least.

In a recent development, it was also confirmed on Monday that Genoa striker Colombo has suffered an injury to the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) of his right knee. Again, an exact recovery time has not been specified, but his injury is the most serious of the three and some reports suggest that his 2026-27 season could be over.

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of news from or pertaining to Germany on November 12, 2026:.

Luxury automaker Mercedes-Benz is halting investment at its facilities in Germany, a board members announced on Thursday.

Mercedes-Benz is "forced to examine, in concrete and detailed terms, which sites in Germany we can still afford to maintain," board of management member Britta Seeger remarked in an interview published on the firm's intranet.

Germany's major IG Metall trade union has enabled the possibility of longer warning strikes amid difficult negotiations for industrial employees.

"The board of IG Metall has pave the way for 24-hour warning strikes in the metalworking and electrical industry," the union mentioned on Thursday.

The union accuses employers of intransigence after three rounds of negotiations without clear progress.

On Wednesday, regional chapters appealed for authorization for full-day warning strikes — the last step before a full union vote and an indefinite labor dispute.

Recent findings suggest that "This escalation is completely excessive and counterproductive," Udo Dinglreiter, the president of the employers' umbrella organization, Gesamtmetall, said. He said that hundreds of thousands of jobs could be at risk.

IG Metall's first chairperson Christiane Benner countered that "the employers want to turn this round of collective bargaining into a dispute over principles." Another union official noted they were offering what amounted to a real-terms pay cut rather than seeking solutions.

IG Metall is calling for a 5% pay increase and other improved conditions for some 3.7 million workers starting in November, while employers have offered a one-off payment in 2027 coupled with a 1.3% increase starting in the summer of 2028.

The union estimates that around 464,000 employees took part in the initial wave of warning strikes that were limited to periods of hours, rather than full days.

Employers argue that they're treading a difficult line between trying not to cut jobs and meeting calls for improved pay amid widespread industrial sector layoffs in Germany in recent years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, 'Tis the season, already. Preparations are underway around Germany and in several cities, Christmas markets are opening to the public.

Some markets are already open in Essen and in Hamburg, Duisburg's opens on Thursday, and Cologne's follows a day later.

The coupons.de website has sought to track the planned prices for mulled wine or Glühwein as the markets open their doors nationwide.

It has been revealed that the bad news? These prices are rising like so many others. The better news? The year-on-year increase is actually smaller than overall inflation figures, at around 1%.

Sources indicate that on average, a cup is liable to set you back around €4.60 (roughly $5.10). Not entirely surprisingly, Munich tops the nationwide pricing chart, with the price peaking at €7. Other sites nationwide tend not to have the gall even to charge 6 euros.

Bargain hunters determined to get the best value mulled wine will need to venture deep into the center of Germany — hardly its core tourist hub — to find the lowest prices starting at around €3.50.

In a recent development, deposits for the cup, the "Pfand," are also only going in one direction, and in the meantime range from €1 all the way up to €5. But there's a strong argument, particularly with the better designs or after a memorable trip, that this can be money well spent as a memento!

Police in the Emsland region in the northwest near the border to the Netherlands have reported a major fire in a complex of residential and commercial buildings in Papenburg.

The fire broke out on Wednesday afternoon, police mentioned the following morning, causing damages worth "at least €10 million ($11 million)." Several hundred emergency services personnel were deployed.

"Based on current findings, the fire broke out in the sauna area of a gym facility on site, and quickly spread to further parts of the complex of buildings," police wrote.

Two men were in the sauna at the time and initially tried to douse the flames but without success.

Police noted the buildings were evacuated as the fire spread, with some surrounding buildings also being cleared as a precaution because of possible smoke-related dangers.

Several people were injured, police said, including the two men in the sauna area suffering mild burns and suspected smoke inhalation sickness. They were treated in a nearby hospital but soon discharged.

"There were also injuries among the first responders," police wrote. "Four police officers, two firefighters and members of the rescue teams suffered mild injuries, particularly via smoke inhalation.".

Recent findings suggest that the fire was only extinguished late on Wednesday night, several hours after it started. The area is sealed off, with possible risks of damaged buildings collapsing. Police have also launched investigations into the fire's cause, but remarked that at present, the area was not safe for that work to start at full scale.

Germany's largest credit bureau Creditreform has published its "2026 Debtors' Atlas.".

Recent findings suggest that it finds that 10.16% of German adults, or 7.36 million people, exhibit at least the early warning signs of excessive debt. A year ago the ratio was 9.74%.

"The financial situation of private consumers has further deteriorated," Patrik-Ludwig Hantzsch, Creditreform's head of economic research, noted. "In particular, the sharply increased living costs, energy costs and housing costs are straining expenditures.".

Hantzsch remarked employment was also becoming an glitch once more, saying "above all, well-paid jobs in manufacturing industries have been cut back in large numbers in recent months.".

The report also highlights rising cases of signs of excessive debt prior to legal action being taken, such as payment reminders or warnings being sent, saying "consumers are taking on more credit-financed expenditures — increasingly also for smaller purchases — at simultaneously rising interest rates.".

A larger share of men than women have excessive debts, perpetuating a longstanding trend.

People around the middle of their working lives, aged 30-39 and 40-49, are most likely to be affected — but the cohort with the fastest-rising share of people with excessive debts are young adults below the age of 30.

Bremen, Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt and North Rhine-Westphalia were among the states with the highest rates of excess debts, while the wealthy and fiscally conservative states of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg had the lowest levels.

Germany's main DAX stock market index has cleared the 27,000-point mark for the first time in its history in morning trading.

It climbed by around 1.3% in order to pass the milestone.

A combination of some positive outlook data from major companies, not least engineering giant Siemens, and the falling oil prices of recent days have helped fuel the uptick.

Siemens' shares had risen by almost 5%, to just over €291 (around $323) each, helping to spur on the gains and making the manufacturer the morning's top performer.

Despite several years of low growth and recession in the German economy, the DAX, like many Western indices, is now trading twice as high as it was prior to the COVID pandemic.

Hundreds of police officers searched apartments and meeting sites for the biker group "Gremium MC" in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg early on Thursday.

The state interior ministry remarked the operation was part of a move to outlaw three sub-chapters of the group, the ones based in Böblingen and Leonberg, as well as the "Gremium MC Chapter Nomads Bosphorus Türkiye.".

Recent findings suggest that this last group was highlighted as a meaningful part of Gremium MC by security officials. It describes itself on Facebook as a great example that "people of different cultures and faiths can be strong together," featuring images of men posing with knives and other weapons.

Gremium MC prominently incorporates into its iconography the symbol of the Prussian military medal for exceptional valor, the Iron Cross, which was discontinued after World War I, reintroduced by Adolf Hitler during World War II, and then scrapped for good.

State Interior Minister Manuel Hagel was expected to make further comments later in the day in Ludwigsburg.

Gremium MC is deemed an "outlaw motorcycle gang" in Baden-Württemberg's latest security report, a term used for biker groups that do not recognize the state monopoly on the use of force and are often tied to organized crime.

"Extortion, drug dealing and pimping in particular tend to be part of their activities," state authorities say.

Baden-Württemberg counts 154 biker chapters in the state with around 2,000 members.

Founded in 1972 in Mannheim, various chapters of Gremium MC across the country have faced legal problems in recent years. In 2021, another chapter in the southwest, Gremium MC Southgate in Heidelberg, was outlawed on suspicion of organized crime activity.

Police in Hanover reported early on Thursday that three men were injured by an unknown driver in a car in the nearby town of Ronneberg.

One person sustained severe injuries in the incident late on Wednesday, police noted.

Two of the wounded were taken to a nearby hospital while the other could be cared for at the scene.

According to recent reports, police said the driver fled the scene and that a search operation was ongoing. Authorities were also still investigating a potential motive for the apparent attack.

Today's updates start with a focus between the southwestern Kurpfalz and Swabian regions, where police have released major morning raids against a biker gang.

According to recent reports, the state Interior Ministry in Baden Württemberg has outlawed three of its chapters. Hundreds of police officers mobilized in the early hours of the morning.

The major IG Metall trade union is planning further strikes in the carmaking sector and other metalworking industries, with an announcement anticipated later in the day.

To the north, near Hanover, police report an apparent car attack injuring three men overnight.

And in the spirit of offering the public service journalism people are truly thirsting for, we'll have some info on the average and localized pricing of mulled wine or Glühwein at Christmas markets this year, as the early birds start to open their doors to visitors. (Yes, already!).

Stay tuned for updates on all this and anything else of note in or pertaining to Germany as the day progresses.

Sources indicate that it is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

It has been revealed that liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

It has been revealed that “There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”.

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso noted. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”.

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

What are fossil fuels?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life.
  • The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.
  • They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

Industry observers note that with 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Right now, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national looks.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres stated.
